sections.title: Atomic Number, Proton Number and Nucleon Number

blocks.t: Mosely's Work — Discovery of Atomic Number

Moseley worked on the frequencies of X-rays (waves with short wavelength but higher energy). He discovered that when different elements were bombarded with cathode rays, X-rays of some characteristic frequencies were produced.

Frequency of emitted radiation  ∝  Z²
√(frequency)  ∝  Z

(where Z = atomic number of the element)

blocks.label: Mosely's Law (Note Wording)
blocks.text: The frequency of emitted X-ray waves is directly proportional to the square of atomic number.

blocks.head: Results of Mosely's Experiment
items: Each element has a specific frequency of emitted X-ray radiation.
Each atom has a specific and different atomic number.
No two elements have the same atomic number.
Atomic number is a fundamental property of an element.

blocks.head: Why Mosely Matters
blocks.body: Before Mosely, elements were ordered by atomic mass (Mendeleev) — creating anomalies like Co/Ni being swapped. Mosely proved that atomic number, not mass, is the true fundamental property. This fixed all periodic table anomalies. The Modern Periodic Law is a direct consequence: properties repeat as a function of atomic number.

blocks.t: Atomic Number vs Mass Number

rows: Equal to sum of protons and neutrons
Nucleon number · almost equal to mass of nucleus

blocks.label: Nucleon Number (Book Definition)
blocks.text: The number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom is collectively called its nucleon number (A), also known as mass number.

blocks.t:
A = Z + N      (Mass number = Protons + Neutrons)
N = A − Z      (Neutrons = Mass number − Atomic number)
Z = A − N      (Protons = Mass number − Neutrons)

Quick rule:
  If Z is even  →  A ≈ Z × 2
  If Z is odd   →  A ≈ (Z × 2) + 1
Symbolic Representation

blocks.head: Nuclear Symbol Format
blocks.body: Standard notation: AZX where A = mass number (top left), Z = atomic number (bottom left), X = element symbol. For ions, charge appears top right. Example: ²⁷₁₃Al → A=27, Z=13, N=27−13=14 neutrons.

blocks.head: Counting Electrons in Ions
items: Cation (positive ion, loses e⁻): Electrons = Protons − charge. E.g., Al³⁺: e = 13 − 3 = 10
Anion (negative ion, gains e⁻): Electrons = Protons + charge. E.g., Cl⁻: e = 17 + 1 = 18
Neutrons never change when an ion forms — only electrons are gained or lost.

blocks.t: Board format: 'Element X has Z=17, A=35. Find p, n, e. If X forms X⁻, find electrons.' → p=17, n=18, e=17. For X⁻: e=17+1=18. Protons and neutrons unchanged.

items.q: Calculate number of neutrons in: (i) ³⁹₁₉K   (ii) ³⁵₁₇Cl   (iii) ⁴⁰₁₈Ar
items.ans:
(i) ³⁹₁₉K: N = A − Z = 39 − 19 = 20 neutrons

(ii) ³⁵₁₇Cl: N = 35 − 17 = 18 neutrons

(iii) ⁴⁰₁₈Ar: N = 40 − 18 = 22 neutrons

items.q: Which of electron, proton, and neutron is deflected the most in the magnetic field?
items.ans: Electron — it has the highest charge-to-mass ratio. Both electron and proton carry the same charge magnitude (1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C), but the electron is 1836 times lighter than the proton → deflects at the greatest angle.

sections.title: Effect of Electric Field on Fundamental Particles

blocks.head: Key Rule (Note Wording)
items: Charged particles (proton, electron) are affected by electric and magnetic fields → deflected.
Neutral particles (neutron) are unaffected → travel in a straight path.

blocks.t: If beams of electrons, protons and neutrons pass at the same speed through an electric field:

items: Neutrons — no charge → no deflection → travel straight perpendicular to field direction.
Protons — positively charged → deflected toward the negative terminal (positively charged).
Electrons — negatively charged → deflected toward the positive terminal (negatively charged).

blocks.t: Angle and Radius of Deflection

Angle of deflection  ∝  charge / mass
  Order: proton  <  electron  (electron deflects at LARGER angle)
  Reason: same charge but electron is 1836× lighter → higher charge/mass ratio

Radius of deflection  ∝  mass / charge
  Order: α-particle  >  proton  >  electron  (electron curves most sharply)
  Reason: α-particle has mass ≈ 4 amu → barely curves (large radius)

blocks.head: Why Electron Deflects MORE Than Proton
blocks.body: Both proton and electron carry the same charge magnitude (1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C). But the electron is 1836 times lighter. Since angle ∝ charge/mass, the electron has a far higher ratio → deflects at a much greater angle and with a much tighter curve (smaller radius).

blocks.t: Penetration Power of Subshells

blocks.head: Penetration Power (From Notes)
blocks.body: Penetration power is the ability of an electron to get close to the nucleus. Higher penetration = stronger nuclear attraction on that electron.

blocks.t:
Penetration power  ∝  1 / l-value
  Order:  s > p > d > f
  (s electrons penetrate most; f electrons penetrate least)

Consequence: nucleus holds s electrons most tightly
  → s electrons hardest to remove from a given shell

blocks.head: Why Penetration Explains Be > B Anomaly
blocks.body: Be's outermost electron is in 2s (high penetration, close to nucleus, held tightly). B's outermost electron is in 2p (lower penetration, shielded by 2s, held less tightly). Even though B has more protons, its 2p electron is easier to remove → IE(Be) > IE(B).

blocks.t: 'Which fundamental particle is deflected most in electric field?' → Electron. For radius order: α-particle > proton > electron. For angle order: electron > proton (neutron = 0).

sections.title: Ionization Energy and Evidence for Electronic Shells

blocks.t: ⚠️ Section 2.3.1 (Atomic Spectra) is DELETED from smart syllabus. Only 2.3.2 is retained.
The space around the nucleus where electrons are distributed is called energy levels. Evidence for these energy levels can be given by using ionization energy.

blocks.label: Ionization Energy (Note Wording)
blocks.text: The amount of energy required to remove 1 electron from the valence shell of an isolated gaseous atom.

blocks.label: Successive Ionization Energies (Note Wording)
blocks.text: The sequence of ionization energies required to remove all electrons of an atom — one by one — until only the nucleus is left.

blocks.head: Key Facts
items: Number of successive IEs = number of electrons in the atom (Li has 3; Be has 4; Mg has 12)
All ionization energies are highly endothermic — always positive (energy must be supplied)
Each successive IE is always greater than the previous one

blocks.t:
X     →  X⁺  + e⁻     ΔH_i1  (1st IE)
X⁺   →  X²⁺ + e⁻     ΔH_i2  (2nd IE)
X²⁺ →  X³⁺ + e⁻     ΔH_i3  (3rd IE)
... continue until nucleus alone remains
Factors Affecting Successive IE (From Notes)

Successive IE  ∝  1 / n-value             (outer shell → lower IE)
Successive IE  ∝  1 / distance (nucleus to electron)
Successive IE  ∝  positive charge on ion  (more positive → holds remaining e⁻ tighter)
Successive IE  ∝  proton / electron ratio  (more p per remaining e⁻ → stronger pull)
Explanation with Magnesium (Z=12) — Most Important

blocks.head: Setup
items: Mg: Z = 12, total electrons = 12
Number of successive IEs = 12 (one per electron)
Electronic configuration: K(2), L(8), M(2) → 3 shells
After removing all 12 electrons, only the Mg nucleus remains

blocks.head: Reading the Graph — Two Jumps
items: Electrons 1 & 2 (3rd shell/M shell): Small gap between IE₁ and IE₂ — both from the same outermost shell → relatively low energy required.
1st big jump between IE₂ and IE₃: The 3rd electron must come from the 2nd shell (L shell) — much closer to nucleus, much higher Z_eff → enormous jump.
Electrons 3–10 (2nd shell/L shell): Gradual increase among IE₃ to IE₁₀ — all from the same shell.
2nd big jump at IE₁₁: The 11th electron is from the innermost K shell — right next to the nucleus → another enormous jump.
Small gap between IE₁₁ and IE₁₂: Both in the same K shell.

blocks.head: NOTE ERROR — Page 10 of Handwritten Notes
blocks.wrong: Notes say: '11th and 12th electron are in same shell (outermost)'
blocks.correct: 11th and 12th electrons are in the same shell — but it is the INNERMOST shell (K shell / 1s²), NOT outermost.
blocks.reason: For Mg, the outermost (3rd/M) shell contains the 1st and 2nd electrons to be removed. The 11th and 12th are the LAST to be removed, from the K shell (closest to nucleus). The note confusion arises from describing them as 'same shell' — correct — but the parenthetical 'outer/most' is wrong. Page 11 of notes correctly states 'first and second electrons are in same shell' and Mg = K(2), L(8), M(2).

blocks.head: Conclusion from Mg Successive IE Data
items: 1st shell (K) has 2 electrons — confirmed by 2nd big jump
2nd shell (L) has 8 electrons
3rd shell (M) has 2 electrons — confirmed by 1st big jump

blocks.t: Beryllium Example (Z=4)

₄Be = 1s², 2s²  →  4 electrons, 2 shells

ΔH_i1  <  ΔH_i2  <<  ΔH_i3  <  ΔH_i4
                   ↑
               JUMP here (between 2nd and 3rd IE)
Reason: 3rd electron enters K shell (much closer to nucleus)
Jump after 2nd electron confirms Be has 2 valence electrons → belongs to Group 2.
First IE Variation — Across Period and Down Group

cards.down_note: No. of shells increases → shielding increases → nucleus holds outer e⁻ less tightly → easier to remove

cards.across_note: Shell number stays same, but proton number increases → nucleus attracts valence e⁻ more strongly → harder to remove. Alkali metals = lowest; noble gases = highest in each period.

blocks.head: Z-Effect (Effective Nuclear Charge)
blocks.eq:
Z_eff  ∝  Z (more protons = stronger pull)
Z_eff  ∝  1 / shielding electrons (more inner e⁻ = weaker pull on outer e⁻)

IE  ∝  Z_eff  (higher effective nuclear charge → higher IE)
IE  ∝  1 / distance  (closer electron → higher IE)
IE  ∝  1 / n-value  (lower shell → higher IE)
blocks.note: Going across a period: same shell, proton count rises → Z_eff rises → IE rises. Going down a group: new shells added → more shielding → Z_eff felt by outer electrons drops → IE drops.

blocks.t: Q5(a) Long Q structure: (1) Define successive IE + equations, (2) State: no. of successive IEs = no. of electrons, (3) Mg: Z=12, 12 electrons, 12 successive IEs, (4) Explain 2 jumps (M→L shell after 2nd; L→K shell after 10th), (5) Conclusion: K(2), L(8), M(2). Graph: x-axis = no. of electrons removed, y-axis = log₁₀(IE).

items.q: Write equations for: (i) 1st IE of Ca (ii) 3rd IE of K (iii) 2nd IE of Li (iv) 5th IE of S
items.ans:
(i) Ca(g) → Ca⁺(g) + e⁻   ΔH_i1

(ii) K²⁺(g) → K³⁺(g) + e⁻   ΔH_i3

(iii) Li⁺(g) → Li²⁺(g) + e⁻   ΔH_i2

(iv) S⁴⁺(g) → S⁵⁺(g) + e⁻   ΔH_i5

items.q: For Al (Z=13), describe the sketch graph of log₁₀(successive IEs) vs number of electrons removed.
items.ans:
Al = 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p¹ → K(2), L(8), M(3)

  • Electrons 1–3 (M shell): low IEs, gradual rise
  • 1st big jump between 3rd and 4th IE (M→L shell change)
  • Electrons 4–11 (L shell): higher IEs, gradual rise
  • 2nd big jump between 11th and 12th IE (L→K shell)
  • Electrons 12–13 (K shell): very high IEs

items.q: ΔH_i1 and ΔH_i2 (kJ/mol) given: I=(2372,5251), II=(520,7300), III=(900,1760), IV=(1680,3380). Identify: (i) reactive metal (ii) reactive non-metal (iii) noble gas (iv) metal forming AX₂
items.ans:
(i) Reactive metal → Element II
IE₁=520 (very low) + huge jump to IE₂=7300 → 1 valence electron → alkali metal (Group 1)

(ii) Reactive non-metal → Element IV
IE₁=1680 (high), IE₂=3380 → non-metal character with multiple valence electrons (likely Group 16/17 behaviour)

(iii) Noble gas → Element I
IE₁=2372 matches Helium exactly. Very high IE₁ with large IE₂ → completely filled shells.

(iv) Metal forming AX₂ → Element III
IE₁=900, IE₂=1760 (both relatively low, close together), large jump expected after 2nd → 2 valence electrons → Group 2 → forms MCl₂

blocks.label: Quantum Numbers (Note Wording)
blocks.text: The set of numerical values that explain the electron position and behaviour around the nucleus is called Quantum Numbers (Q.N.).

blocks.t: These are solutions of Schrödinger's wave equation (HΨ = EΨ). Three quantum numbers arise from this equation (n, ℓ, m). A 4th (spin) was added later. Together they tell us: (i) position of electron, (ii) shape of path, (iii) orientation along 3 axes.
(1) Principal Quantum Number (n)

blocks.label: Principal Quantum Number (Note Wording)
blocks.text: The quantum number that explains the main energy level around an electron around the nucleus is called Principal Quantum Number (P.Q.N.).

blocks.head: Characteristics of n
items: Represented by 'n'
Value always positive integer — never negative and never zero
n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5... (designated K, L, M, N, O shells)
It is unidimensional (describes one property at a time)

blocks.head: Significance of n — 6 Points
items: (i) No. of shells: No. of shells = n-value (K=1, L=2, M=3, N=4; also P-shell n=5, Q-shell n=6, R-shell n=7)
(ii) Energy of electron: E ∝ n² — as n increases, energy of electron in that shell increases
(iii) Distance from nucleus: Distance ∝ n² — larger n = electron farther from nucleus (K shell nearest; M shell farther away)
(iv) Size of atom: Size ∝ n-value — size of atom increases with increase in n-value
(v) No. of electronic clouds (max electrons): Formula = 2n² (K=2, L=8, M=18, N=32)
(vi) First IE: IE ∝ 1/n-value — increase in n-value → decrease in first IE (outer shell → easier to remove)

blocks.t: (2) Azimuthal Quantum Number (ℓ)

blocks.label: Azimuthal Quantum Number (Note Wording)
blocks.text: The quantum number that explains the formation of fine spectrum is called Azimuthal Quantum Number (A.Q.N.). It explains the shape of the path around the nucleus.

blocks.head: Formation of Fine Spectrum (Why ℓ Exists)
blocks.body: A line spectrum passed through a high-resolving monochromator splits further into smaller lines called 'fine spectrum'. This means there are some sub-energy levels inside the main energy levels → subshells. The azimuthal quantum number describes these subshells.

blocks.head: Characteristics of ℓ
items: Represented by 'ℓ'
Value depends on value of n: total values = n-value
Values: ℓ = 0 to (n−1)
Values may be zero — never negative

blocks.head: Importance/Significance of ℓ — 5 Points
items: (i) Angular nodes: No. of angular nodes = ℓ-value   (ℓ=0→0 nodes; ℓ=1→1 node; ℓ=2→2 nodes; ℓ=3→3 nodes)
(ii) Nature of subshells: ℓ=0 → s-subshell (sharp); ℓ=1 → p-subshell (principal); ℓ=2 → d-subshell (diffused); ℓ=3 → f-subshell (fundamental)
(iii) Shape of subshells: Shape determined by nodes. ℓ=0→s→spherical; ℓ=1→p→dumbbell (2 lobes); ℓ=2→d→cloverleaf/sausage-like (4 lobes); ℓ=3→f→flower-like
(iv) Penetration of electrons: Penetration ∝ 1/ℓ-value → order: s > p > d > f
(v) No. of electrons in subshell: Calculated by 2(2ℓ+1) → s=2, p=6, d=10, f=14

blocks.head: *Note on Lobes
blocks.body: No. of lobes ≈ 2×ℓ for p, d, f (p=2, d=4, f=6). The d<sub>z²</sub> orbital is a special case — it has 2 lobes along the z-axis plus a torus (doughnut ring) in the xy-plane.

blocks.t: (3) Magnetic Quantum Number (m)

blocks.label: Magnetic Quantum Number
blocks.text: The magnetic quantum number 'm' describes the orientation of an orbital in space, within a subshell. It explains the magnetic behaviour of electrons and the splitting of spectral lines of fine spectrum in a magnetic field.

blocks.head: Characteristics of m
items: Represented by 'm'
Value depends on value of ℓ: number of m values = (2ℓ+1)
Values: −ℓ to +ℓ (may be 0 and negative) — range: −ℓ … 0 … +ℓ
Total values = 2ℓ+1 (gives number of degenerate orbitals)

blocks.head: Significance of m — 2 Points
items: (i) No. of electrons: Each orbital has 2 electrons at maximum (each m-value = 1 orbital = max 2e⁻)
(ii) Maximum orbitals in shell: Total orbitals = n² (calculated by summing all m-values in shell)

blocks.head: Degenerate Orbitals
blocks.body: Degenerate orbitals: Orbitals with the same shape and same energy — called D.O. No. of degenerate orbitals = (2ℓ+1). In the absence of magnetic field, all orbitals within a subshell have identical energy. In a magnetic field, they split — this is why the quantum number is called magnetic quantum number.
items: Probability of finding e⁻ depends on no. of degenerate orbitals: Probability ∝ no. of degenerate orbitals
s: m=0 (1 orientation); p: m=−1,0,+1 → px, py, pz; d: m=−2,−1,0,+1,+2 → dxy, dxz, dyz, dx²-y², dz²

blocks.t: (4) Spin Quantum Number (s)

blocks.label: Spin Quantum Number (Book + Note)
blocks.text: It explains the self-rotation of an electron about its own axis. According to electromagnetic theory, a spinning charge generates a magnetic field, causing an electron to behave like a magnet. Represented by 's'.

blocks.head: Characteristics of Spin
items: Up-spin: s = +½ → anticlockwise rotation → represented by ↑
Down-spin: s = −½ → clockwise rotation → represented by ↓
Two electrons in an orbital always have opposite spins (one ↑, one ↓)
Three quantum numbers describe an orbital; the 4th (spin) distinguishes two electrons in the same orbital

blocks.t:
Incorrect set of QN: n=3, ℓ=3, m=0 is INVALID because for n=3, ℓ can only be 0, 1, or 2 (max ℓ = n−1 = 2).
4th electron of Be: Be = 1s²2s² → 4th electron is in 2s. n=2, ℓ=0, m=0, s=−½ (opposite spin to 3rd electron).

items.q: What information about an electron can be obtained from: (i) n (ii) ℓ (iii) m (iv) s
items.ans:
(i) n (Principal): Size and energy of the orbital/shell; distance from nucleus; max electrons = 2n²

(ii) ℓ (Azimuthal): Shape of the orbital/subshell; nature of subshell (s/p/d/f); penetration power

(iii) m (Magnetic): Spatial orientation of the orbital in space; number of degenerate orbitals

(iv) s (Spin): Self-rotation direction of electron (+½ anticlockwise ↑ or −½ clockwise ↓)

items.q: If n=2 and ℓ=1, how many orientations in space are possible?
items.ans: ℓ=1 → m = −1, 0, +1 → 3 orientations (px, py, pz along x, y, z axes)

items.q: If n=3 and ℓ=2, which shell and subshell does the electron belong to?
If ℓ=2, find all possible values of m and maximum number of electrons.
items.ans:
ℓ=2 → m = −2, −1, 0, +1, +2 → 5 values of m (5 orbitals)
Max electrons = 2(2ℓ+1) = 2(5) = 10 electrons

blocks.label: Atomic Orbital (Book Definition)
blocks.text: An atomic orbital is defined as the three-dimensional region in space around the nucleus in which the probability of finding the electron is maximum.

items.body: 1 orbital (ℓ=0, m=0). Electron density uniformly distributed in all directions around nucleus. Size increases with n: 1s < 2s < 3s. Zero angular nodes.
3 orbitals (ℓ=1, m=−1,0,+1): px, py, pz oriented along x, y, z axes — mutually perpendicular. 1 angular node (nodal plane through nucleus). All three are degenerate.
5 orbitals (ℓ=2): dxy, dxz, dyz, dx²-y², dz². 2 angular nodes. All five degenerate. dz² is special: 2 lobes along z-axis + torus ring in xy-plane.

blocks.head: Shape and Nodes Connection (From Notes)
items: No. of angular nodes = ℓ-value → s has 0 nodes (sphere), p has 1 (nodal plane), d has 2, f has 3
f-subshell has 7 orbitals (ℓ=3, m=−3 to +3) — shapes are very complicated
Shape determined by nodes — more nodes = more complex shape
Orbitals with same ℓ value in same shell are degenerate (same energy, different orientation)

blocks.head: What s, p, d, f Stand For
blocks.body: The letters come from spectral line appearances: s = sharp, p = principal, d = diffused, f = fundamental.

blocks.t: 'There are 3 orientations of p-orbital due to 3 values of m. Justify.' → For p-subshell: ℓ=1 → m = −1, 0, +1 → 3 distinct values → 3 different spatial orientations (px, py, pz along x, y, z axes). These are degenerate (same energy) but different orientations. Hence 3 values of m justify 3 orientations.

items.q: What does an orbital represent according to the wave mechanical model?
items.ans: An atomic orbital is the 3-dimensional region in space around the nucleus in which the probability of finding the electron is maximum. It does not represent a definite path — unlike Bohr's model — but describes the probability distribution of the electron's location.

items.q: There are three orientations of p-orbital due to three values of magnetic quantum number. Justify.
items.ans:
For the p-subshell, ℓ = 1. The magnetic quantum number m can take values from −ℓ to +ℓ:
m = −1, 0, +1 → three distinct values.

Each value of m represents a different spatial orientation:
m = +1 → px (along x-axis)
m = 0 → pz (along z-axis)
m = −1 → py (along y-axis)

These three orbitals are mutually perpendicular (90° apart) and degenerate (same energy). Hence, three values of m justify three orientations of p-orbitals.

blocks.label: Electronic Configuration (Book Definition)
blocks.text: Electronic configuration is the distribution of electrons among available shells, subshells, or orbitals of an atom or ion.

blocks.t: Requirements to Write Electronic Configuration (From Notes)

items: Atomic number of element
Charge on ion (+ve or −ve) if applicable
Energy level of shell: E ∝ n² → lower n = lower energy = filled first
Maximum space for electrons: Shell (2n²); Sub-shell 2(2ℓ+1); Orbital (max 2 electrons each)
Aufbau Principle and n+ℓ rule for subshell order
Pauli's Exclusion Principle and Hund's Rule for orbital filling

blocks.t: 2.6.1 Distribution of Electrons in Shells
Filling order: K(n=1) < L(n=2) < M(n=3) < N(n=4) — lower n-value = lower energy = filled first.
2.6.2 Distribution of Electrons in Subshells — Three Rules

blocks.label: Aufbau Principle (Book Definition)
blocks.text: This principle says that the subshells in an atom are filled with electrons in an increasing order of their energy values. Also known as the building-up principle.

blocks.head: The (n + ℓ) Rule for Subshell Energy Order
blocks.body: Energy of a subshell depends on (n + ℓ). Fill in order of increasing (n + ℓ). If two subshells have equal (n + ℓ), fill the one with lower n-value first.
blocks.eq:
1s  2s  2p  3s  3p  4s  3d  4p  5s  4d  5p  6s  4f  5d  6p  7s

n+ℓ values:
1s=1 · 2s=2 · 2p=3 · 3s=3 · 3p=4 · 4s=4 · 3d=5 · 4p=5 · 5s=5 · 4d=6

Key: 4s (n+ℓ=4) fills BEFORE 3d (n+ℓ=5)
     3d (n+ℓ=5) fills BEFORE 4p (n+ℓ=5) because n=3 < n=4

blocks.label: Pauli's Exclusion Principle (Book Definition)
blocks.text: No two electrons in an atom can have the same values for all the four quantum numbers. Or: Two electrons in an orbital will always have opposite spins.

blocks.label: Hund's Rule (Book Definition)
blocks.text: When degenerate orbitals are available and more than two electrons are to be placed in them, they should be placed in separate orbitals with the same spin rather than in the same orbital with opposite spins.

blocks.head: Why Hund's Rule? (Physics Reason)
blocks.body: When electrons occupy the same orbital, they are in the same region of space → maximum electron-electron repulsion → higher energy. When they spread into different degenerate orbitals with same spin, they stay farther apart → less repulsion → lower energy → more stable. Nature always favours the lowest energy state.

blocks.t: Key Electronic Configurations — Important Elements

rows: Paired e⁻ in one 2p — spin-pair repulsion

blocks.head: Cr and Cu Exceptions — Why d⁵ and d¹⁰ Are Special
items: Cr (Z=24): Expected [Ar]3d⁴4s² but actual is [Ar]3d⁵4s¹. One electron shifts from 4s→3d because half-filled 3d (3d⁵) is extra stable (exchange energy + symmetry).
Cu (Z=29): Expected [Ar]3d⁹4s² but actual is [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹. Fully-filled 3d (3d¹⁰) is extra stable → one electron from 4s completes the d subshell.
Rule from Notes: If d has 4 or 9 electrons, shift one electron from 's' to 'd' to achieve stability.
3 states of subshells: Completely filled (most stable) > Half filled (extra stable) > Partially filled (least stable)

blocks.head: How E-Configuration Helps Us (From Notes)
items: (i) Period number of element: Equal to number of shells
(ii) Group number of element: Usually equal to valence electrons
(iii) Nature of element: Metal or non-metal (position in PT)
(iv) Reactivity of elements
(v) Blocks of elements: s-block (Groups 1–2), p-block (Groups 13–18), d-block (transition), f-block (lanthanides/actinides)

blocks.t: Free radicals (Section 2.8) and Semiconductors (Section 2.9) are DELETED from smart syllabus. Brief note: A free radical is a species with one or more unpaired electrons (e.g., Cl· = 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁵).

items.q: Write e-configs for ₄₈Cd and ₅₇La using noble-gas cores.
items.ans:
₄₈Cd: [Kr] 4d¹⁰5s²   (Kr=Z=36; add 4d¹⁰5s²)

₅₇La: [Xe] 5d¹6s²   (Xe=Z=54; 4f is not yet filling at La)

items.q: Write the complete electron configuration for antimony ₅₁Sb.
How many unpaired electrons in each atom of ₅₁Sb?
items.ans:
Valence shell: 5s²5p³
5s: ↑↓ (paired)
5px: ↑ · 5py: ↑ · 5pz: ↑ (all singly occupied by Hund's rule)
3 unpaired electrons

items.q: Write valence shell orbital diagrams for ₁₃Al, ₁₄Si, ₂₈Ni
items.ans:
₁₃Al (3s²3p¹): [3s: ↑↓] [3px: ↑] [3py: ] [3pz: ] → 1 unpaired

₁₄Si (3s²3p²): [3s: ↑↓] [3px: ↑] [3py: ↑] [3pz: ] → 2 unpaired (Hund)

₂₈Ni ([Ar]3d⁸4s²): 3d has 8 electrons in 5 orbitals → [↑↓][↑↓][↑↓][↑][↑] → 2 unpaired electrons

items.q: Element: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d¹⁰4s²4p⁶4d¹⁰5s²5p⁵. Find: (i) block (ii) group (iii) period (iv) name.
items.ans:
(i) Block: p-block (outermost subshell being filled is 5p)

(ii) Group: Group 17 (VIIA) — 7 valence electrons: 5s²5p⁵

(iii) Period: Period 5 — outermost shell n=5

(iv) Element: Iodine (I) — Z=53

items.q: Element: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d⁵4s¹. Find block, group, period, name.
items.ans:
Block: d-block (3d subshell is being filled)
Group: Group 6 (VIB) — 6 valence electrons (3d⁵ + 4s¹)
Period: Period 4 (outermost shell n=4)
Element: Chromium (Cr) — Z=24 (exception: 3d⁵4s¹ for stability)

mcqs.q: The quantum number 'm' of a free gaseous atom is associated with:
opts: The effective volume of the orbital
The spatial orientation of the orbital
The energy of the orbital (no magnetic field)
mcqs.exp: 'm' is the magnetic quantum number → describes orientation in space. 'n' → size/energy; 'ℓ' → shape; 's' → spin.

mcqs.q: When 3d subshell is completely filled, the next entering electron goes into:
mcqs.exp: Filling order: ...3d < 4p... After 3d is full (n+ℓ=5), next is 4p (n+ℓ=5, lower n=4 wins over 4d with n+ℓ=6).

mcqs.q: Quantum number values for 2p orbitals are:
mcqs.exp: '2p' means n=2 (2nd shell) and p-subshell which has ℓ=1.

mcqs.q: An electron having: n=4, ℓ=0, m=0 and s=+½ lies in:
The quantum number values (n, ℓ, m) for the 4th electron of ₄Be atom are:
mcqs.exp: Be = 1s²2s². 4th electron is 2nd in 2s: n=2, ℓ=0 (s-subshell), m=0 (only one s orbital), s=−½.

mcqs.q: The correct order of first ionization energies is:
mcqs.exp: He (noble gas, highest); F (most electronegative in period 2); N > O (N has half-filled 2p anomaly); O; Mg (metal, lowest of these five).

mcqs.q: A p-orbital has a characteristic shape with how many lobes?
mcqs.exp: A p-orbital has 2 lobes — one on each side of the nucleus along its axis (dumbbell shape).

mcqs.q: The three p-orbitals in a given energy level are oriented:
opts: Mutually perpendicular along x, y, z axes
mcqs.exp: px, py, pz are mutually perpendicular (90° apart) along the three Cartesian axes.

mcqs.q: How many d-orbitals are there in a given energy level?
mcqs.exp: For d-subshell: ℓ=2 → number of orbitals = 2ℓ+1 = 2(2)+1 = 5. (f has 7: 2(3)+1=7)

mcqs.q: What information does the principal quantum number (n) give about orbitals?
mcqs.exp: n gives size and energy of the orbital. Shape → ℓ. Orientation → m. Spin → s.

mcqs.q: How many unpaired electrons are present in a cobalt atom (Z=27)?
mcqs.exp: Co = [Ar]3d⁷4s². In 3d⁷: filling 5 orbitals by Hund's rule → ↑↓ ↑↓ ↑ ↑ ↑ → 3 unpaired electrons. The book marks 'c' (Four) which appears to be a book error. Correct answer = 3 unpaired (b).

mcqs.q: The maximum number of electrons in the 3rd shell is:
Successive ionization energies provide evidence for:
mcqs.exp: Large jumps in successive IE values indicate transitions between electron shells — direct evidence for the shell model.

mcqs.q: An element has IE data: I₁=520, I₂=7300 kJ/mol. This element most likely belongs to:
mcqs.exp: Huge jump after 1st electron (I₁=520 low, I₂=7300 enormous) → only 1 valence electron → Group 1 (alkali metal). I₁=520 matches Potassium.

sqs.q: There are three orientations of p-orbital due to three values of magnetic quantum number. Justify.
sqs.a:
For the p-subshell, ℓ = 1. The magnetic quantum number m can have values from −ℓ to +ℓ, giving: m = −1, 0, +1 — three distinct values.

Each value of m represents a different spatial orientation:
m = +1 → px (along x-axis)
m = 0 → pz (along z-axis)
m = −1 → py (along y-axis)

These three orbitals are mutually perpendicular (90° apart), degenerate (same energy), but different orientations. Hence three values of m justify three orientations of p-orbitals.

sqs.q: 'I₃' of Mg is much bigger than its 'I₂'. Justify.
sqs.a:
Mg (Z=12) has electronic configuration: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s² → shell distribution: K(2), L(8), M(2).

I₁ and I₂ remove the 2 electrons from the outermost (3rd) shell (M shell). These electrons are far from the nucleus and well-shielded → relatively low energy needed.

I₃ requires removing the 3rd electron, which is now from the 2nd shell (L shell / 2p subshell) — much closer to the nucleus, less shielded, experiencing a much stronger nuclear pull.

Additionally, Mg²⁺ has achieved a stable noble-gas configuration (isoelectronic with Ne) → breaking into this stability requires enormous extra energy.

Therefore I₃ shows a very large jump compared to I₂.

sqs.q: Among Li, K, Ca, S, Kr — which has lowest first IE? Which has highest?
sqs.a:
Lowest IE: Potassium (K)
K is an alkali metal in Period 4 (Group 1). It has the largest atomic size among these, with 4 shells and strong shielding. Its single 4s¹ valence electron is far from the nucleus and weakly held → easiest to remove.

Highest IE: Krypton (Kr)
Kr is a noble gas in Period 4 with a completely filled outer shell (4s²4p⁶) → extremely stable configuration → requires enormous energy to remove an electron.

Approximate order: K < Ca < Li < S < Kr

sqs.q: (i) Write full electronic configuration of K (Z=19). (ii) Explain why 4s fills before 3d.
sqs.a:
(i) Full configuration of K:

K = 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s¹

(ii) Why 4s fills before 3d (Aufbau / n+ℓ rule):

Energy of a subshell is determined by (n + ℓ):

  • 4s orbital: n + ℓ = 4 + 0 = 4
  • 3d orbital: n + ℓ = 3 + 2 = 5

Lower (n + ℓ) = lower energy = fills first. Therefore 4s (sum=4) has lower energy than 3d (sum=5) → 4s fills first, despite having higher principal quantum number.

sqs.q: (i) Element X has Z=17, A=35. Find p, n, e. (ii) X forms X⁻. Find p, n, e.
sqs.a:
(i) Neutral atom ³⁵₁₇X (Chlorine):
Protons = Z = 17
Neutrons = A − Z = 35 − 17 = 18
Electrons = Z (neutral) = 17

(ii) X⁻ ion (Cl⁻):
Protons = 17 (unchanged — nuclear charge never changes)
Neutrons = 18 (unchanged)
Electrons = 17 + 1 = 18 (gained 1 electron)

sqs.q: (i) State general order of filling orbitals up to 4p. (ii) Explain why 4s fills before 3d.
sqs.a:
(i) General filling order (up to 4p):

1s → 2s → 2p → 3s → 3p → 4s → 3d → 4p

(ii) Why 4s fills before 3d:

Using (n + ℓ) rule:

  • 4s: n+ℓ = 4+0 = 4 (lower sum = lower energy)
  • 3d: n+ℓ = 3+2 = 5 (higher sum = higher energy)

4s has smaller (n+ℓ) value → lower energy → fills first according to Aufbau principle.

sqs.q: For Al: I₁=580, I₂=1815, I₃=2740, I₄=11,600 kJ/mol. (i) Account for trend. (ii) Explain large increase I₃→I₄. (iii) List Al ions in increasing size.
sqs.a:
(i) Trend in ionization energies:
Successive IEs increase because each electron is removed from a progressively more positive ion. As electrons are removed, the remaining electrons experience the same nuclear charge but less electron-electron repulsion → pulled in more tightly → harder to remove each subsequent electron.

(ii) Large increase from I₃ to I₄:
Al = 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p¹ → outer shell (3rd shell) has 3 electrons.
I₁, I₂, I₃ remove these 3 outer electrons.
I₄ removes the 4th electron from the 2nd shell (2p) — much closer to nucleus, shielded by only 1s² → experiences much higher effective nuclear charge → enormous energy required. This confirms Al has 3 valence electrons (Group 13).

(iii) Increasing size of Al ions:

Al < Al⁺ < Al²⁺ < Al³⁺ ← WRONG ordering

Correct: Al³⁺ < Al²⁺ < Al⁺ < Al
As more electrons are removed, fewer electron-electron repulsions remain → electrons pulled in closer by same nuclear charge → each successive ion is smaller.

sqs.q: I₃ of Mg is much bigger than its I₂. Justify.
sqs.a: Same as SAQ b above. The key point: I₁ and I₂ come from the outermost M shell; I₃ comes from the L shell (much closer to nucleus) → large jump in energy required.

sqs.q: Why is the IE of Li much lower than He despite Li having higher nuclear charge?
sqs.a:
Reason 1 — Shell number: Li's valence electron is in the 2nd shell (farther from nucleus) while He's electrons are in the 1st shell (very close).

Reason 2 — Shielding in Li: The 1s² core electrons shield Li's 2s electron from the full +3 nuclear charge → Z_eff felt by Li's outer electron is only ~+1.3.

Reason 3 — He's stability: He has a completely filled 1st shell — both electrons experience the full +2 charge with no shielding → very stable → very high IE.

lqs.title: Q3 (Descriptive) — Quantum Numbers
lqs.q: What are quantum numbers? Describe briefly principal and spin quantum numbers.

parts.label: INTRODUCTION — Quantum Numbers
points: Definition: The set of numerical values that explain the electron position and behaviour around the nucleus is called Quantum Numbers
These are solutions of Schrödinger's wave equation (HΨ = EΨ)
Three quantum numbers describe an orbital (n, ℓ, m); 4th (spin) distinguishes two electrons within same orbital
They describe: (i) position of electron, (ii) shape of path, (iii) orientation along 3 axes

parts.label: PRINCIPAL QUANTUM NUMBER (n)
points: Explains the main energy level of an electron around the nucleus
Values: n = 1, 2, 3, 4... → designated K, L, M, N shells
Always positive integer; never zero or negative
Describes size and energy of the orbital
Larger n = greater distance from nucleus = higher energy = less tightly bound
Max electrons in shell = 2n² (n=1→2, n=2→8, n=3→18, n=4→32)
IE ∝ 1/n-value (increase in n → decrease in first IE)

parts.label: SPIN QUANTUM NUMBER (s)
points: Explains the self-rotation (spin) of an electron about its own axis
Spinning charge generates magnetic field → electron behaves like a magnet
Two possible spin states: s = +½ (anticlockwise, ↑ up-spin) or s = −½ (clockwise, ↓ down-spin)
Two electrons in same orbital must have opposite spins (Pauli's Exclusion Principle)
Three quantum numbers describe an orbital; 4th (spin) is needed to distinguish two electrons in same orbital

lqs.title: Q4 (Descriptive) — Shapes of Orbitals
lqs.q: Draw the shapes of s, p, and d-orbitals. Justify by keeping in view the azimuthal and magnetic quantum numbers.

parts.label: s-ORBITAL (ℓ=0, m=0 — 1 orbital)
points: Shape: Spherical — electron density uniformly distributed in all directions
ℓ=0 → only one value of m (m=0) → only 1 orbital; no directional preference
0 angular nodes → perfectly spherical
Size increases with n: 1s < 2s < 3s

parts.label: p-ORBITALS (ℓ=1, m=−1, 0, +1 — 3 orbitals)
points: Shape: Dumbbell (2 lobes on opposite sides of nucleus along one axis)
ℓ=1 → m = −1, 0, +1 → 3 degenerate orbitals: px, py, pz
Three orbitals are mutually perpendicular (90° apart) along x, y, z axes
1 angular node (nodal plane passing through nucleus)
All three p-orbitals have equal energy (degenerate) in absence of magnetic field

parts.label: d-ORBITALS (ℓ=2, m=−2,−1,0,+1,+2 — 5 orbitals)
points: Shape: Cloverleaf/double dumbbell — more complex
ℓ=2 → m = −2, −1, 0, +1, +2 → 5 degenerate orbitals
Five types: dxy, dxz, dyz, dx²-y², dz²
dz² is unique: 2 lobes along z-axis + a doughnut (torus) ring in the xy-plane
2 angular nodes
Present from 3rd shell onwards (n=3, ℓ=2 minimum)

lqs.title: Q5 (Descriptive) — Successive IE of Mg
lqs.q: What do you mean by successive ionization energies? How is the electronic shell structure of magnesium (Mg) derived from successive ionization energies?

parts.label: DEFINITION AND EQUATIONS
points: Successive ionization energies: the sequence of energies required to remove all electrons from an atom one by one until only the nucleus remains
X → X⁺ + e⁻ (ΔH_i1); X⁺ → X²⁺ + e⁻ (ΔH_i2); X²⁺ → X³⁺ + e⁻ (ΔH_i3) ... and so on
Number of successive IEs = number of electrons (Li=3, Be=4, Mg=12)
All IEs are highly endothermic (always positive); each successive IE > previous

parts.label: MAGNESIUM EXAMPLE (Z=12)
points: Mg has 12 electrons → 12 successive IEs
Electronic configuration: K(2), L(8), M(2)
Electrons 1 & 2: removed from 3rd (M) shell → low IEs, small gap between them
1st JUMP between IE₂ and IE₃: 3rd electron enters L shell (much closer to nucleus → big energy increase)
Electrons 3–10: removed from 2nd (L) shell → gradual increase in IEs
2nd JUMP between IE₁₀ and IE₁₁: 11th electron enters K shell (right next to nucleus → enormous jump)
Electrons 11 & 12: removed from 1st (K) shell → very high IEs, small gap between them

parts.label: CONCLUSION AND GRAPH DESCRIPTION
points: Two large jumps confirm electrons exist in 3 distinct energy levels (shells)
1st jump after 2nd electron → M shell has 2 electrons → Mg is in Group 2
2nd jump after 10th electron → L shell has 8 electrons; K shell has 2
∴ Mg = K(2), L(8), M(2) — confirmed by successive IE data
Graph: x-axis = number of electrons removed (1-12); y-axis = log₁₀(IE); shows two clear discontinuities (jumps)

quiz.q: Mosely observed that √frequency of emitted X-rays is directly proportional to:
quiz.exp: Mosely's Law: √frequency ∝ Z (atomic number). This proved atomic number — not mass — is the fundamental property.

quiz.q: Number of neutrons in ³⁹₁₉K is:
quiz.exp: N = A − Z = 39 − 19 = 20 neutrons.

quiz.q: Which fundamental particle is deflected the MOST in an electric field?
quiz.exp: Electron has the highest charge/mass ratio (same charge as proton but 1836× lighter) → deflects at greatest angle.

quiz.q: Radius of deflection in an electric field follows the order:
quiz.exp: Radius ∝ mass/charge. α-particle has largest mass → largest radius; electron has smallest mass → smallest radius (sharpest curve).

quiz.q: Penetration power of subshells follows the order:
quiz.exp: Penetration ∝ 1/ℓ-value. s(ℓ=0) has highest penetration; f(ℓ=3) has lowest. s electrons are held most tightly by nucleus.

quiz.q: Ionization energy of Beryllium (Be) is HIGHER than Boron (B). This is because:
opts: Be's 2s subshell is fully filled — extra stable
Be has smaller atomic size only
quiz.exp: Be (1s²2s²) has fully-filled 2s — extra stable. B (1s²2s²2p¹) has its outermost electron in 2p which is shielded by 2s² and at higher energy → easier to remove.

quiz.q: Magnesium (Z=12) has successive ionization energies. The FIRST big jump occurs between:
quiz.exp: Mg has 2 valence electrons in M shell. After removing I₁ and I₂ (both from M shell), I₃ must come from the L shell (much closer to nucleus) → big jump.

quiz.q: If successive IE data shows a large jump after the 3rd electron, the element belongs to:
quiz.exp: Large jump after 3rd electron = outer shell has 3 electrons = 3 valence electrons = Group 13 (like Al).

quiz.q: The principal quantum number (n) gives information about:
quiz.exp: n describes size and energy of the orbital. Shape → ℓ. Orientation → m. Spin → s.

quiz.q: For an electron in 3d subshell, the correct quantum numbers are:
quiz.exp: '3d' means n=3 (3rd shell) and d-subshell (ℓ=2).

quiz.q: The azimuthal quantum number (ℓ) for an electron in 4f subshell is:
quiz.exp: f-subshell always has ℓ=3 (regardless of which shell). s=0, p=1, d=2, f=3.

quiz.q: How many degenerate orbitals are in the d-subshell?
quiz.exp: d-subshell: ℓ=2 → number of orbitals = 2ℓ+1 = 2(2)+1 = 5.

quiz.q: The magnetic quantum number (m) describes:
quiz.exp: m (magnetic quantum number) describes the spatial orientation of the orbital. It explains why p-orbitals have 3 orientations (px, py, pz).

quiz.q: The spin quantum number s=+½ represents:
quiz.exp: s=+½ = anticlockwise spin = ↑ (up-arrow). s=−½ = clockwise spin = ↓ (down-arrow). This is the book convention.

quiz.q: Which of the following sets of quantum numbers is INVALID?
quiz.exp: For n=3, ℓ can only be 0, 1, or 2 (max ℓ = n−1 = 2). ℓ=3 is impossible when n=3.

quiz.q: Shape of s-orbital is:
quiz.exp: s-orbital (ℓ=0) has a spherical shape — electron density uniformly distributed in all directions around nucleus.

quiz.q: The electronic configuration of Cr (Z=24) is:
quiz.exp: Cr is an exception: [Ar]3d⁵4s¹. One electron shifts from 4s to 3d because half-filled 3d (3d⁵) is extra stable.

quiz.q: The 4th electron of Beryllium (₄Be) has quantum numbers:
quiz.exp: Be = 1s²2s². 4th electron is 2nd in 2s orbital: n=2, ℓ=0, m=0, s=−½ (opposite to 3rd electron which has s=+½).

quiz.q: According to Hund's rule, when filling three electrons in three p-orbitals:
opts: Two go in same orbital, one in another
All three go in same orbital
Each goes in separate orbital with same spin
Each goes in separate orbital with opposite spins
quiz.exp: Hund's rule: fill degenerate orbitals singly with same spin first before pairing. So 3 electrons → px(↑), py(↑), pz(↑).

quiz.q: Which element is likely in Group 2 based on successive IE data showing a large jump after the 2nd electron?
quiz.exp: Large jump after 2nd electron → outer shell has 2 electrons → 2 valence electrons → Group 2. Mg (Z=12) with K(2), L(8), M(2) is a perfect example.
